utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. May we have the witness? May we have the witness? (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Edina Residovic, I appear on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. With me is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zejnil Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Zdravko Mucic. My co-counsel, Mr. Michael Greaves, is still indisposed. With me is my colleague Duric, attorney from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Salih Karabdic, appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic, with me is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can you warn the witness he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Sudar, may I remind you you are still under oath. BRANKO SUDAR (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey, I think you are continuing your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Sudar, how are you today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I hope you slept well knowing you are going to be going home soon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind you of our agreement that we had yesterday that you would testify in this court about the things you personally know, personally saw, personally heard and you were just reminded, of course, that you were under oath and I know you will follow our agreement. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do follow our agreement. I am saying only what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You were moved from -- I know can you cannot remember dates, but you were moved from Musala back to Celebici because it was determined you had surrendered an automatic weapon, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not surrender any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You did testify before last week that you had purchased a pistol; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A pistol, yes, and I left it at home and I told them where it was and then they went there the next day and found it. I did buy myself a pistol and I had that pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: On last Thursday on page 5764, line 2 of the record, you said that you did not know the guards but that you may have seen a person known as Zenga as a child. You stated you did not know him. The truth is that you found out who Zenga or Mr. Landzo was from the other people; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not seen him -- rather I had seen him but I did not know him well before, and I saw him in the camp, they called him Landzo, Zenga, he was no longer a child. He was a young man.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Sudar, I believe you said that you testified -- that you served in the Yugoslav army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what rank you had in the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no rank, I did not want to have any rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You were an ordinary soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: As an ordinary soldier you are forced to or it is mandatory that you follow the orders of your superiors, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I did not have any superiors or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You have testified that Mr. Landzo would call people out of hangar number 6 and it would be fair to say that as far as you know, he could have been merely following orders; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whose orders he was following, but he did call people out. On whose orders, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Is it not true that most of the time, 90 per cent of the time, that the people were taken out of hangar number 6, it was at night and it was dark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would happen in daytime. If I were to tell the whole story, I would need half a day. He would call one after another. I just mentioned some of the specific cases, for instance Babic, Mrkajic, then the taxi driver Bendjo, there were people who were taken out in the daytime and he would come into the hangar in the daytime and beat people, not only at nighttime.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also testified on page 5757, line 5 of the transcript from last Thursday that the door of hangar 6 was always kept shut, making it unbearably hot inside; is that not what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door was closed when they wanted it to be closed, when they wanted us not to have enough air. We would lie down on the concrete to get more air. We had no water, no food, or very little, and when they came in, they would open the door, Zenga opened the door when he came in. Sometimes it was open, but sometimes when he wanted to torture us, then the door was closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is also true that most of the guards were very young; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not say they were that young. As soon as they were carrying a weapon and is a soldier, I do not think a child can wear a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It is true and you know that Mr. Landzo was only about 18 or 19 years old in 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I do not know how old he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You say you heard his voice most often because he was the one who was ordered to call the people out. There were other young guards that may have had high pitched voices too, is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His voice was generally heard. There was Dedic Osman as well, let me remember, Padalovic, there was a policeman from Foca, Dedic, Osman somebody called Kemal, I do not remember the surnames very well but Landzo was seen most often, at least as far as I was able to observe, he was the most prominent in everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I would just like for you to listen to this question. I think it is a real simple answer. It is true that you do not know the voices of all of the other young guards, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other young guards -- I have forgotten these things, but I remember his high pitched voice. It was easily recognisable. As soon as we would hear his voice, we knew it was Zenga. He would walk around the hangar, he would bring in a dog, he would force it to jump on people, but the dog did not want to luckily. He would set it against us. He did all kinds of things. It is difficult to describe from the human point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: But my question was, I appreciate you telling your story, but my question was: you do not know the voices of all the other young guards, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance Kemo or Osman, we would hear the voices. But it is five years since that. I would know when Delic was coming too, one can hear these voices and recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You talked last Thursday about a man named Scepo Gotovac and I just want you to listen to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Scepo Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You told your story last Thursday but I have one specific question. The specific question is Mr. Gotovac was taken outside the hangar and you did not see what happened to him outside the hangar, you only saw the results when he was brought back inside the hangar; is that not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga took him out of the hangar. Delic was there, just outside the door, they took him out, one could hear him wailing, Zenga was beating him, one could hear his voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Sudar, the truth is you do not know what was happening outside because you did not see it, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the door was open, we saw him take him out, and in front of the door one could hear him being hosed with water.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to take you back now to a Simo Jovanovic. I want you to remember that on page 5769, line 3, you did tell this court that he was beaten by his neighbours, and I believe his neighbours were from Celebici, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people or other, I heard, I did not know them well, somebody called Subasic and there was a Cosic, something like that, they were teasing him; Simo, do you want some fish, because he had a fish pond apparently. Zenga was with them too.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I want to also ask you the story you told us last Thursday, that Zenga came in and he started beating some people which included Bosko Samoukovic. At that time, when Mr. Samoukovic was hit and he fell down, Mr. Landzo seemed frightened about that, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember these details. When the man fell, to tell you the truth, I could not even stand to watch any more. He first beat Rajko Mrkajic, and Samoukovic's son, I think his name was Nedzo, then he hit Bosko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Sudar, my question was: did Mr. Landzo seem frightened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. You do not know whether Mr. Landzo was following orders at that time, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say. It is up to each individual whether they will follow orders or not, each one is responsible for himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You also told us about a Spaso Miljevic and you went into detail about some yellowish gun powder that was put on the blade of a knife and heated inside the hangar. My question to you is: if Mr. Miljevic told this court that all this happened outside the hangar, he would be wrong, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was some way away from me. I saw him being mistreated inside and out. He hit him inside and Babic, the forester and Gotovac, both outside and inside, all kinds of things, I cannot recall all the specific details.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Also if this person said the knife was heated outside by setting a linen bag on fire he would be wrong also? It had nothing to do with the gun powder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that something yellow was powdered on him, that is what this man told us afterwards when he had these burns.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but you told this court on Thursday that you saw this yellowish powder and this yellow liquid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was carrying some yellowish powder, he was carrying it and a liquid too. I do not understand these things, these flammable materials, I do not know much about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sudar. I do not have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, a couple of very short questions, your Honour. Mr. Sudar, yesterday, Mr. Moran, Defence counsel, asked you some questions about a list being called out of names of people to leave the camp and your name was on that list. Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Yesterday, when you were being cross-examined by Mr. Moran from the Defence, he asked you about Mr. Delic coming into the hangar and calling out a list of names of people to be released from the camp. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you not respond to your name being called out because you wanted to stay in the camp, or was it more because you wished to be exchanged by the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to be exchanged by the Red Cross because I had been registered, and before that, Zivak, who had been in the camp was released and afterwards we heard he had been killed, so I was afraid. I thought I would be protected by the Red Cross by the very fact that I had been registered by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in fact later exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was later exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is all for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sudar. You are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You are calling your next witness now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, the Prosecution is now calling Mr. Petko Grubac. Petko Grubac (sworn)

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Petko Grubac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your place and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 20th October 1939 in the vicinity of Pluzine, Montenegro, in the municipality of Polje Crkvicko.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Serb, a Montenegran.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your profession, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a doctor, specialist in neurology and psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you please summarise your education, Dr. Grubac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed elementary school and then secondary school, a grammar school, then I studied medicine at the school of medicine in Sarajevo. After that I completed my specialisation at the Clinical Hospital in Sarajevo, in psychiatrics and neurology and afterwards, I did a postgraduate course in health care and I worked in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where were you living in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Precisely where did you work at that time, in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in the health centre as a neuro-psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you left Konjic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the situation in Konjic, somewhere around the second half of April 1992 I took my son and daughter to the family home of the parents of my wife in the village of Bradina where they had their home and farm, and during the weekend for May day, my wife and I went to visit my children, though we were both working in Konjic all that time. After the May day holidays we would go to work by bus or in our own car to Konjic, and we were in Konjic for the last time on 5th or 6th May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After that, you went to Bradina, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that I stayed with my family in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you be more precise about the reason for which you left Konjic for Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left Konjic because I did not feel safe, because some things started happening in Konjic which provoked fear in me and my family. On May day 1992, a man, a Serb, was killed, Djordjo Magazin in his courtyard and his house was close to the orthodox church, and some other things started happening so that we were fearful and we felt that perhaps it would be better for us to stay in the family home of my wife's parents in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, was there any organised armed defence in the village of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I cannot tell you in detail what was happening, but I think there were some kind of village guard duty, I would call it that, and they held certain checkpoints in the surroundings of Bradina in order to prevent anyone coming into the village to kill somebody, set fire to something and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you in any way part of this organisation of checkpoints, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at the beginning I was in my in-laws' home and later on I worked in the infirmary as a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any weapon, were you armed anyhow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had no weapons. Actually, I do not know how to use any armaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you part of any political organisation there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until 1990 I was a member of the league of communists, as the majority of the people there were, and after that I tried with a group of people of Croats and Muslims to organise some sort of a movement, a movement for Yugoslavia, but that did not take off so I was actually not a member of any political party after that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you part of any negotiations going on between persons from Bradina and persons from Konjic in that area at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not directly a participant but there was a group of people who went to the village of Podorosac to consult with the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see. Dr. Grubac, was there any military action in Bradina in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean on the part of the Serb population, whether they undertook any actions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am meaning if there was any kind of military action, attack, fight in Bradina in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In May 1992, someone, I am not quite sure who, mined the tunnel which was a communication line in Bradina and Konjic and I believe that from May 10th, on May 10th there was some sort of a smaller scale attack but I am not sure on whose part it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about in the later part of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later in May, on May 25th, there was an attack on Bradina by the Muslim and the Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where were you at the time of this attack on Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the village infirmary with my colleague, Mrkajic Relja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At some point were you captured or arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not captured, nor was I arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened exactly to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day when the attack on Bradina took place, somewhere towards evening, some people came, called me and my colleague to dress the wound of a man who had been wounded in the nearby hamlet. We went there, took a look at this person. He was wounded in the upper leg. We bandaged his wound, we gave him some pain killers and then we returned to the infirmary. In the evening I went to sleep in the house of my wife's parents in a hamlet on the opposite side from the infirmary. There I stayed the night and there I was that night and on the next day, 26th May, when the attack on Bradina continued. From that position we could roughly see what was happening in the other parts of the village. We could hear the fire, we could see houses being set on fire, and this continued on 26th, then 27th May, and they conditionally speaking were sweeping the village. They were setting houses on fire, and also the house where I had been staying with my family. We were afraid that they would kill someone, that they would do something to someone so that one evening on the 26th, we spent the night at the house and on the 27th, with some other women and children who were fleeing from the village as refugees, we slept by a creek, on the 27th, that night and as we saw them advancing, they had advanced to this hamlet and were setting houses on fire in that hamlet. We were in fear for our lives and on the next morning we decided to come down to the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I wanted you to slow down a little and go ahead in your account, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this group of refugees there were about 30 women, children, and four of us men. We decided to take the road to the centre of the village to go to the checkpoint, the army and report to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: To which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the Muslim and Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After you reported to them, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the checkpoint we found the army and the police. There they separated the women and the children and took them to the village school and the four of us men were put in a car and taken to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly where in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the police building, the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened to you in this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First they seized -- my things are there, I had a briefcase with my personal things and documents, which they took. That was at the entrance gate. Then they took me inside the building to a corridor where I stayed for a while. There they separated us. The three other men were taken somewhere and they kept me for a short while in that corridor. Soon thereafter, the commander of the MUP appeared, the head of the MUP, Jasmin Guska, with his assistant Niksic and several other policemen. He started cursing at me and insulting me and he slapped me in the face and he ordered the policemen to take me to a cell. They took me to a cell then, in the cellar. There I found seven or eight, perhaps even ten people. I recognised some of them. They told me that these were people from Celebici, the village of Celebici, that they had been incarcerated there for three weeks. They looked pitiful, miserable, unshaven, dirty, starved, emaciated. They were thin. I could hardly recognise some of them. Among them was also Simo Jovanovic. That was a room that I mentioned, perhaps 3 by 4 metres. At one end there was planks and there were old army blankets on the planks. They told me they had been sleeping and sitting there for three weeks. In another corner there was a plastic or metal container which they used to relieve themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you remain in this room with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For two hours maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that some policemen came, told us to get out of that cell. They also assembled the people from another adjacent cell, also people who have been imprisoned there from the village of Celebici. They all loaded us into a police van and shut us inside, told us not to try to escape or else, and then they took us somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Exactly where were you brought with this van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the Celebici camp, to a building of the former Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, did anybody tell you why you were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one told me anything, nor did they feel the need to explain anything to me because at that time Serbs were being arrested without any reason. I believe that just being a Serb was reason enough for them to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Again, you told the court now that somebody took your personal belongings and your documents from you. Did you ever get them back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never. I never got those things back, although later at a certain occasion when I was shut up in the same building again, yet another time, I asked for those things to be returned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many prisoners were with you in the van which brought you to Celebici that day, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 20 prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember, by the way, which day that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a minute. It was 28th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately at what time of that day did you arrive at Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere around noon or immediately thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did the van stop inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The van passed through the metal gates of the camp. It came to a halt at a certain spot near the gate post and a wall, at a clearing which was some 15 or 20 metres from the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened right after the van stopped in this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They opened the rear door of the van. They told us to get out and to stand against a wall, to place our arms behind our heads, to lean against a wall with our arms and to spread our legs and also to empty our pockets. Excuse me, they also told us to take our belts out of our trousers, those with belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you stay lined up against this wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between half a hour and a hour, perhaps more likely a hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How were you treated while staying lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were not physically maltreated or beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where were you taken after you were lined up against the wall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to a building, a hangar, the so-called number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many people did you observe being present in hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were around 250 people in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By the way, without giving details now, how long did you -- how many nights did you spend inside hangar 6 approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two nights.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Going back to the moment you arrived there, what happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, and anyway, what happened to you the next day after your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day after our arrival, nothing in particular happening, but in the evening, somewhere around 10.00 pm or perhaps a bit later, the guard opened the door to the hangar and called me out to get out, called my name to get out, so I did, I went out. He put me in some kind of a van, in the rear. He shut the door and drove off with me inside. Then he stopped, having brought me to the building where the camp command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you were brought with a car inside the camp to the command building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened to you when you reached the command building in this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They led me inside the command building and then into a room to the right of the entrance, in which room I saw, I found my colleague, Dr. Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic, who was the President of the war presidency and also the chairman of the SDA party in Konjic. With him was Jasmin Guska, who was the police commander or the head of the Ministry of the Interior in Konjic and secretary of the SDA party. With them was also Hazim Delic who was the assistant warden of the camp in Celebici or deputy warden.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened there in this room with these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dr. Hadzihuseinovic asked Delic to leave the room and he did. They put me on a chair and they interrogated me, asking me why I had been brought, why I had been in Bradina, who I associated with before, whether I had any connections with the army, with the officers. Eventually, Dr. Hadzihuseinovic told me in the end, that is, that I would be treated by them according to the Geneva convention, saying that afterwards I would be tried for what I had done. Jasmin Guska saw my glasses in my pocket and told me to throw them on the floor and he trampled them underfoot and he broke them, and then he cursed at me, swore at me. He told me to sit on the floor, crawl on the floor and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By the way, did you ever receive back your glasses or another pair of glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jasmin Guska stepped on the glasses before my eyes. They were on the floor, so he broke them. I did not get them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just to give us some general information, can you see well enough even without glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see well, these were for short sightedness, if I were to drive for any long periods, and they were shaded a bit and I used them mostly when it was strong sunshine. I was comfortable wearing them driving. I did not at all times wear glasses, only sometimes, on such occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did exactly Rusmir Hadzihuseinovic say about you being supposed to be treated according to the Geneva Convention? Can you be more precise about what he told you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only say that he told me that they would treat me in accordance with the Geneva Convention, and I cannot say what he meant by that. I am not -- I do not know whether he knew what it meant, treating a doctor who is a prisoner or in a camp according to the Geneva Conventions because obviously later they did not at all treat me as a doctor according to the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the command building in this occasion? How long did all this last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not last long. It perhaps lasted 45 or 60 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you then go back to hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they placed me in the same van and returned me to hangar 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you spend that night in hangar 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened to you the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The following day someone came for me. I could not exactly say who, and took me to the building of the elementary school called "3 Mart" in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As we understand, that was after two nights spent in the camp then on May 30th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you brought to the 3rd March school with a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken there in a vehicle because it is some 4 or 5 kilometres away from Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was in that vehicle? Only the driver or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall that detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did anybody tell you what would be your task in the school named 3rd March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know remember anyone telling me what I was supposed to do in the school 3rd March, but when I came there I found my colleague Dr. Relja Mrkajic and he told me we would be there with the injured people to extend assistance to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you have arrived there and you found your colleague Relja Mrkajic. How many patients did you find there right on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the number of patients have any variation in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It changed. Some came and a number of the patients were shifted to another building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What kind of patients were they? Can you briefly give us a general overview of the problems or injuries they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all severely injured patients. I do not know according to what criterion they had been chosen and taken up there, but they had grave injuries, fractures or severe injuries. One of them was in a coma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did any of these patients tell you where and how did they get their injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember some specific persons who told you where he had got his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, Marko Mrkajic told me that his leg had been broken when he was being taken to the Celebici camp. Strajo Cecez had a jaw fracture and he also told me he had been hurt when he was being brought to the camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: All this is relevant for us? We are more concerned with what happened in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, because we are now coming to a particular person who is in the indictment as a victim of wilful killing in our indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you remember approximately how many persons there were with severe injuries from Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what criterion to apply, a judicial one or medical, to say whether these are grave or light injuries, but the criterion which I can apply is the one which is used in court in my country to tell you which of the injuries were light and which were grave --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am sorry, I just wanted to know the number of people with injuries from the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe all these people were from Celebici camp, perhaps some of them were not, but most of them were from Bradina and Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. During your stay in the 3rd March school did any of the patients die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one patient died.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is the name of this patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Slobodan Babic himself able to say anything about how he received his injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, from the moment I arrived to 3rd March school Slobodan Babic could not speak and it was not possible to communicate with him verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Slobodan Babic already there when you arrived in 3rd March school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe in detail the visible injuries which were visible on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I was able to observe was bruises. He was black and blue on his face, neck, arms. My colleague told me that he had an injury in his mouth. I opened his mouth with a spatula and I looked inside. He had an injury of the hard and soft palate which was slightly bleeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you treat Slobodan Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Babic was seriously injured. He was in a coma and what we could do was to place urinary catheter because he could no longer control his urination so as to avoid him being always wet. We had one catheter and we had it implanted -- we had some antibiotics, penicillin. We gave him strong doses of penicillin while it lasted and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say that Slobodan Babic had an injury of the hard and soft palate, do you mean -- which kind of an injury did you see looking at his mouth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was torn, his whole soft and hard palate was torn and there were pieces of tissue hanging. There was a laceration inside and there was pus and blood dripping from these wounds inside his mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did Slobodan Babic remain in a coma before dying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ever since I arrived, that is from 30th until maybe the 5th, I think, 5th June roughly. That was when he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was his body immediately removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the body was taken away, I do not know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did your stay at the 3rd March school end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One night, this could have been 6th or 7th June, Pavo Mucic came and told us that we were going to be moved to another place. We asked why and where we were going, and he said that we were being moved to the Celebici camp because we were not safe at the school. That was the reason he gave, because the school could be shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately at what time on that day Mr. Mucic came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came late at night, maybe after 10.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: That was on 6th or 7th June, you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many patients were there in that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that moment there were much fewer patients than at the beginning, because a doctor came from the health centre and he moved half of the patients to the Musala sports hall in Konjic. Just before we were moved somebody told us that the remaining patients should be reduced so that there would be no more than ten patients, plus the two of us doctors, so there were about ten of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So that night when Mr. Mucic came, there were about ten patients. Was Mr. Mucic in uniform when he came that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he come with any vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a large truck with a canvass cover, and I cannot remember for sure whether there was a private car as well, but I know for sure that there was a large lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After Mucic told you that you should move somewhere else, actually to Celebici, what did you do then, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us that we needed to move the things we had, the beds we had, and the mattresses that some of the injured were lying on. We loaded all this on to this large lorry and we climbed up as well and they took us to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were the patients lying or standing in the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were leaning against the mattresses, whatever position they could find, because this was a truck that we had to fit all the things into and all of us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic also come on the truck with you to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall for sure whether Mucic was in the actual driver's cabin or in another vehicle, but he did come to Celebici with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the truck stop inside the camp or at the entrance of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The truck stopped inside the camp in front of building 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told us then that we had to move in to this building. He showed it to us, he opened the metal door --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say "he", who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo, Pavo Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We unloaded the things, we positioned the beds and the mattresses inside building 22, and that is where we stayed from 6th or 7th onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who told you what you were supposed to do in building 22, if anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that officially no one told us anything as to what we would be doing. It was understood what we had to do with the injured people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which capacity did Mr. Mucic come and pick you up and tell you what he told you and transport you to Celebici? Do you know which official role he had, if any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not introduce himself to us officially. He did not say why he had come. He did not say what his official position was. We learnt later what his position in the camp was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you learn about his official position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We learnt from the guards and from the relationships amongst them that he was the commander of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, just to give an immediate overview to the court without entering into details, how long did you stay as a prisoner in Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the Celebici camp from 28th May until 22nd July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Considering all those days you spent in the 3rd March school, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you stay all the time in building number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the time I was in building 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Dr. Relja Mrkajic also spend his time in building number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were together throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe in some detail this building, building number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Building 22 is actually a hangar, but it differed from hangar number 6 as it was not entirely made of metal. The walls were made of building material. It had a metal roof towards the front, the side facing the command building, there was a metal double door. Opposite to the door there were two high windows which could be opened only partly, like a flap. The floor was concrete. When we came into the building it was absolutely empty. The size of the building is about 8 or 10 metres by 5, roughly. We put in the wooden beds that we had, some mattresses that we had brought from the school. I slept on a bed that is normally used in infirmaries, that was in the 3rd March school and we brought it with us. There was no water inside. There was not a toilet inside, nor any other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe in some detail the door of this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The doors were metal, double doors, both wings could be opened. There was a Elset lock. They were mostly closed, but as this was a hangar they did not fit too well. The doors were raised from the ground by about 1.5 to 2 centimetres, which we used to peep out to see what was happening in the yard and in the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about the windows? How many windows were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two windows on the opposite side to the doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So what part of the camp could you see looking through these windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The window that was to the right of the entrance we could see tunnel number 9 and we used that window frequently out of curiosity, but also to learn things, and one of the injured persons who was a patient had a father imprisoned from number 9, so he would spend a lot of time at the window to see what was happening to his father.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was this patient by the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name is Mrkajic, his father's name is Nikola Mrkajic, he was in number 9 and his name was -- I am afraid I cannot recall his first name for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It does not matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I will remember later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please now look at the model you see in front of you. You can stand up, you can even turn around if you wish and examine it and tell the court if you recognise it. You had better keep your earphones, Dr. Grubac. May I ask the usher to provide the witness with a pointer so he can point? What is this, Dr. Grubac? What does this represent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This model represents the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you please point to the particular places you have been talking about, the entrance, the command building, the hangar, building 22, tunnel 9 et cetera, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with this part of this facility, whereas the rest of it I am not familiar with because I did not move about there. It was used -- I am not aware that it was used as a camp, at least I am not familiar with that. This was a segment of the railway track going from the railway station at Celebici and entering the actual facility. This is the entrance to the camp from the village. This is the entrance we use, there may have been another one, but I do not know, but that was where things were happening. This is the wall that I referred to where we were lined up when we were brought in at the beginning. This is the reception where the guards were. Building B is a barracks is a hut used as a command building. Opposite is number 22 where we were, and this building D is also part of the command building where the guards slept. This, I do not know what it was used for, I do not remember it very well. The windows are here and from this window we could see this facility, that is tunnel number 9. Further away here we would go here, to one of these buildings, I think this one was number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Grubac. You can go back to your seat. Going back to the description of building 22, could you please now describe this place in its function as an infirmary. Can you explain the facilities, the equipment, the medicine, the instruments, et cetera, which you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said what the building looked like when we arrived. It was like a hangar. I do not know why it was that we concluded that it was a warehouse for firefighting equipment. I think one of the prisoners said that when they first arrived and were put in that building that there were some fire extinguishers there and that is why we assumed that it was a warehouse for that equipment. So there was no water, as I said, no tap, no toilet. There was electricity, though. We called the building number 22 or we called it the infirmary. Inside were the two of us doctors, Dr. Relja Mrkajic and myself, and there were about ten injured people. When we had no more room on the beds, we had one or two mats that we had brought with us from the 3rd March school, from the gym and these gym mats were also used by the patients instead of beds. Among the equipment we had an office table, a wooden office table, one wooden chair. We had a pressure gauge, a stethoscope. At the beginning, we had a few bottles of penicillin. At the beginning, we had a metal drum with sterile bandages. We had a pair of tweezers which were not sterile. We had some bandages, and later on they gave us old sheets to use as bandages for the patients. This drum with the sterile compresses and gauze could be sterile only until it was opened, after which it was no longer sterile, but we still used it. Later on they did not provide any more sterile material. We had a few plastic syringes and needles. We did not decide who would be brought into the building or who would be taken away; nor could we have any influence regarding the provision of medicines and other materials. We did not have an oxygen apparatus or any other medical equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So could you in any way perform any kind of surgery, and with which instruments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to perform any surgery you have to have the necessary instruments, which necessarily have to be sterile. We had no surgical instruments, and even if we had had them they could not be sterilised. We only had a pair of scissors, surgical scissors with which we cut the gauze and the bandages and on one occasion Dr. Relja did intervene with a patient who had pus on his leg. He used the scissors to open this wound and to clean it, but we could not engage in any other kind of surgical treatment. We could not even provide sterile bandages for people who needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any procedure for requesting and obtaining medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In communication with them they told us there were no instruments or equipment they could provide, but as for the medicines and supplies, I did write up a list several times of what we needed, but Hazim Delic said that it was not available and several times he would bring a couple of bandages, some pain killer tablets, some diarrhoea tablets and a liquid to treat lice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: If you could describe your medicine supply, how many kinds of medicines would you say you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning we had some antibiotics, but only penicillin in small bottles. I think these bottles were 6 million of penicillin. We had a small quantity of this. We had no broad spectrum antibiotics, nor any other kinds of antibiotics. We had some analgesics at the beginning, that is pain killers. We had some pills to treat diarrhoea, as many prisoners had diarrhoea and occasionally we had this liquid for destroying lice. We had no other supplies, no gauze, no bandages, no burn treatment, ointment, because there were lots of people with burns, nor any other sterile material to treat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you send persons to the hospital when you deemed that necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had no power to decide as to the way the injured would be treated, nor when they were brought in or taken away or taken to any other institution, and while we were there not a single of the patients was taken for diagnostic or any other reasons to a medical institution, though the need for this did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were there medical files for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only at the beginning, Dr. Relja and I kept a log. There was a notebook where we would put down the number, the name of the patient, the diagnosis and the treatment we gave. We kept this log at first, believing it to be necessary to have medical documentation as we had been used to, but we saw that this had no interest and that it served no purpose and gradually we gave up.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you in a position to be complete and accurate in keeping these records and writing what you had to there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not dare register every injury because we feared that somebody might come and look into this notebook and that we might have some consequences as a result, so we would enter a lighter diagnosis or something insignificant, mainly leaving out the main cause of the injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who kept these records? It was you or Dr. Relja Mrkajic, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of us, there was not any fixed rule. I think I made more entries than Relja, but he also made entries occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you know which has been the final destination of this notebook? Where was it kept, first of all, at the time you used to fill it in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We kept it on the only table we had. Later on I put it away in one of the drawers. I do not really know what fate it suffered, what happened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Going back to the night when you first arrived at building 22, was the building empty? You said the building was empty when you first arrived there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You told us that you arrived there together with about ten injured prisoners. Did the number of the injured prisoners have a variation in the following days and weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number of the injured did not vary very much because there was not any space but occasionally we would use one of those mats, so that the number was more or less steady, ten and then it would go up to 11 or 12. There was not much variation, but the patients changed within that limited number. There were always ten or twelve of them, but they changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, do you mind if we have a break and come back at 12.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, your Honour. (11.30 am) (A short break) (12.00 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Turone, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Grubac, before the break we were talking about the number of injured prisoners inside building 22. Can you say approximately with what frequency did new injured people, injured prisoners, arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say that it happened following a certain specific definite rhythm or order. They came, I do not know following which system, the injured people came to building number 22. We mainly -- I, myself and Dr. Relja Mrkajic had no say in terms of who was to be brought to the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean about the number of prisoners, very approximately what frequency there was about new comings of people.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To that building prisoners came seeking some kind of medical aid and then they would return to their respective buildings, structures 6 or 9. We would extend the assistance they sought and then they returned to either of those two buildings. Some then came, some of the guards would bring them. Most frequently Delic would bring some people to be hospitalised at the ward or to be in-patients. There would be at the least ten injured people in the ward at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just to give a general overview, what kind of injuries did these people have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had different injuries. They had injuries which had been inflicted with a hard object. They had burns, they had injuries inflicted with firearms or some infections which were consequent to their injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did any of these prisoners die while they were in the infirmary, I mean building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In building 22 two of the injured died.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Petko Mrkajic, Pero, and Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Starting with Mr. Pero Mrkajic, can you say approximately when did he arrive at building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He arrived at building 22 in the month of June, probably in the second half, immediately after the half of the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did he arrive? Was he in a position to walk by himself, or was he brought by other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that after all he could walk. As far as I can remember two of the prisoners from building number 6 slowly, resting every now and then, brought him, and assisted by them he managed to come to building number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did any of these two prisoners accompanying him say anything to you when they brought Pero Mrkajic to the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that they said that they had been ordered by someone to transfer him to building number 22, that he had been beaten, viciously beaten up, and that they could no longer hold him there with the other prisoners, but that they had to transfer him to building 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you put Mr. Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We put Mr. Pero Mrkajic on a mat near the exit from building 22, on the right-hand side from the entrance, on a mat on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Pero Mrkajic conscious when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was conscious when he came.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he in a position to say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was able to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you remember what he said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details, I know that he told me that they had beaten him up and that his injuries had been inflicted in structure number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By the way, did you know Mr. Pero Mrkajic from before? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, I knew him from before. He was a caterer. He had a restaurant in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Had you ever treated him before in your professional capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a disabled person in the sense that he could not see from one eye because of an injury that he had sustained early on in his youth. He would often come to me for some prescriptions for some drugs for himself, for blood pressure, for a cold, for some antibiotics or for his wife who was also a chronic patient, had high blood pressure and was also handicapped because she did not have one leg but had a crutch. She had a prosthesis, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: As far as you know, had Dr. Relja Mrkajic ever treated Pero Mrkajic before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. Relja told me that of late, he had this disorder -- he had sugar diabetes that he could control with tablets. It was not a very serious form of this disease -- was not insulin dependent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe in detail the injuries which were visible on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Mrkajic had many injuries on his body which in fact were large blood haematomata all over his body. He was blue, he had this blood haematomata all over his body. These were the outside injuries. Whether he had any internal ones I was not able to ascertain as I did not have any diagnostic means at my disposal or any method to apply for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you treat Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Practically, we did not treat him to speak of. While he could still swallow we gave him some pain killers and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you treat his diabetes too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we had no medicaments for diabetes, and apart from that we were unable to diagnose the concentration as we had no methods, diagnostic methods to diagnose the concentration of sugar in his blood or his urine and without such data, even if we had had the medicaments we would not have dared give him any without such data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he ever lose consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His condition kept slowly and steadily deteriorating so that in a couple of days he lost consciousness and was in a coma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: After how many days did he die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All in all, perhaps in six or seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Pero Mrkajic have any relative inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had two sons. The two sons of Pero Mrkajic were shut up in building number 9, or rather in tunnel number 9. They are Zara Mrkajic, probably his real name is Jarko and Desko Mrkajic, probably Desimir Mrkajic is his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were these two men allowed to see their father or his body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Pero died Hazim Delic brought both of his sons to building number 22 and he told them "say goodbye to your father".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was the body of Pero Mrkajic immediately removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his body, the body of Pero Mrkajic was left overnight in building number 22 and it was only the next day, that is to say, me and Dr. Relja, took him out. People came with a hearse, put him in that vehicle and took him away. We cleaned the mat to prepare it for another possible injured person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any investigation into the death of Pero Mrkajic, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware that there had been any investigation. As far as we are concerned no one asked us to write some sort of discharge paper or to state the cause or time of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody ever ask you what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you asked to fill out a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that was not the custom at the camp. Neither I nor Dr. Relja ever filled in any death certificates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Let us now talk about Bosko Samoukovic. Can you say approximately when he arrived at building 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosko Samoukovic arrived after Pero Mrkajic. It could be in the middle of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The middle of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, July, possibly in mid July. I am not sure of the exact time. I think it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. How did he arrive? Was he in a position to walk by himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how he arrived, but he could not walk, I know that. I do not know how, in what way he had been brought to the ward. I know that two inmates brought him inside and we had a bed prepared for him and they put him on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody come and see Samoukovic right after his arrival in number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Immediately after that, when we put him in the bed, Hazim Delic came and he said to someone, perhaps he was accompanied by one of the guards, to call Landzo Zio Zenga, immediately to see what he had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, Landzo Zio Zenga did come and looked at the injured person and said to Dr. Relja and myself, "you have to cure him".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean Zio Zenga? Do you mean Esad or Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Zio Zenga. Esad Landzo Zenga. I do not know why I always have confusion with this name instead of Esad Landzo Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember what did Zenga exactly say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he said something to that effect, perhaps it is not completely accurate formulation of the exact words he used, but to that effect, "you must treat him. You must see to it that he recovers".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was Bosko Samoukovic conscious when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was conscious.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he in a position to say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He could say a word or two, but he was in such a serious condition that he was actually struggling for life. He had a hard time breathing. He was out of air. He was blue and red in the face. Later he broke out in sweat all over his face. He kept showing his chest with his hands. Sometimes he tried to sit up from his lying position. One gave the impression that there was a man who was unable to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you remember anything he might have said during all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He moaned, he indicated -- pointed to his chest. I cannot exactly remember whether he articulated any of his thoughts, whether he asked for anything. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember any other detail about the injuries which were visible on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not thoroughly examine his body nor look it over, but massaged his chest several times with his hands. I gather that he wanted to tell me something and I tried to palpate his thorax, his chest and I could feel that it was not as elastic as was to be expected. On pressing, I could hear some sort of a crackling noise and I concluded that his ribs were broken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you treat him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It only lasted for a very short time. Practically, we did not really treat him. We only tried to check whether there was any content in his mouth. We tried to put him in what we referred to as the coma position, lying on his side, to prevent him from suffocating on his tongue or some content in the mouth, but he was so upset, he was gasping for air, that it was hard for us to keep him in that position. I do not remember having given him any drugs or medicaments as we practically had none to treat him with.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did Bosko Samoukovic die?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He died in perhaps 20 or 30 minutes upon arrival at building number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was the body of Bosko Samoukovic immediately removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember the details. I cannot remember whether the body was removed immediately after that, but it did not stay overnight in the building number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any investigation into the death of Mr. Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know there was no investigation, no one asked me anything, nor was Dr. Relja Mrkajic asked anything about the death of Bosko Samoukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you to fill in a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, did you ever treat any prisoners who had burn injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, although this was done more often by my colleague Dr. Relja because this is something that he is more familiar with because he is a specialist for the ear, throat and nose, and he more often treated such wounds, although we were together in the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you anyway remember approximately how many times did that happen, that people came with burn injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came quite often, although we practically had nothing to treat them with. Relja and I myself would remove the scales on their burns, the outer layers and then put a gauze compress -- if we did not have any, we would just bandage it to prevent it from being further infected.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of any prisoners having such burn injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say exactly by name what prisoners had burns and where, but I do know that there were prisoners who had burns on the palms of their hands, on their legs, on their upper and lower legs, some had burns on their faces, ears. I know that a prisoner came called Cakani, that was his nickname. His surname was Bendzo, I do not know what his first name was exactly. Then there was Djordic Kuljanin, but I cannot say where exactly they had burns. This was mainly burns, as we physicians say, of first and partly second degree covering the skin and some subcutaneous tissue in these burns.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You are not in a position to say more details about that, about these people having burns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say the names. I do know that they told us that these burns were inflicted because they had been -- gasoline had been poured on them and then lit, or some flammable bands or tapes or cords, as they refer to them, had been put on them, some things which are used in fireworks or in blowing mines in civil engineering works.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Did you always treat prisoners inside building 22 or were there occasions when you went to hangar 6 or tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both I and Dr. Relja Mrkajic did occasionally go to hangar number 6, to tunnel number 9, and to the reception where the women were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who asked you to go there, or who brought you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently one of the guards would go with us. Sometimes nobody went, we could go ourselves, but more often than not one of the guards would go with us. Who gave them the orders to accompany us there I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say very approximately how many times you had occasion to go to hangar 6 for this reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how many times I went to hangar number 6, but one could put it in the words "often", or quite a number of times; that would be my definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Whenever you went there did you notice there prisoners with visible injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were many prisoners with visible injuries there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you mention any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has just occurred to me, for instance, the name of Simo Jovanovic, probably because I had known that man from before. On one occasion when I went there he was on a kind of a box. He could not move, he was beaten up. He was complaining of not having enough air, that he had pains all over his body and so on. It is difficult to select amongst such a large group of people who were all beaten up, to select any particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you able to treat Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not treat him. His condition required intensive care in a proper medical establishment, but he did not have the good fortune to be transported to such an institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you point out these conditions to anybody?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean officially?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we could not inform anyone officially, nor were we in a position to write up any reports about the condition of the injured people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How many times approximately did you happen to go to tunnel 9 to visit prisoners there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tunnel number 9 was under a special regime, to put it so, so I went there two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember the reason for which you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once I went there because one of the guards came to ask us to examine the prisoners to see whether they needed any medicines. I went there a second time. I was asked to make a list of people there who were suffering from grave chronic diseases and maybe once more between these two visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you notice in tunnel 9 prisoners with visible injuries on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may not be able to describe clearly enough the situation in building number 9. May I describe it, what it looked like, the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish, you can, briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to say that because it is difficult to select any particular injury. It was actually a tunnel which was about 1.5 or 1 metre 20 wide. The height was about 1 metre 50. The ceiling was arched and the whole tunnel was slanting downwards so it was very difficult to walk along it. The prisoners who were there in a half sitting, half lying position, were thrown one on top of the other because of this inclination of the floor, so they could not even stretch out their legs properly.
