Though I am not very tall I also had to bend down to walk and it was difficult to pass, because there was no room between their bodies and between their legs to go to the end of the tunnel. There was a terrible stench inside. One could hardly breathe and at one end they relieved themselves. They were filthy, in a miserable state, extremely resigned to their state. They themselves were not willing to talk about what was happening to them. It is difficult for me to describe now the injuries that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you were asked to write down a list of prisoners of tunnel 9 with very bad conditions, how many people did you list, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not asked at that time to write down the names of people with serious injuries, but rather people with chronic diseases. I assumed they wanted to have a record of people who had been suffering from a disease from before they came, so I was not asked to list the names of people with injuries, but rather people with previous chronic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately how many people did you list, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to report such diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I see. In a general sense, were you permitted to treat whoever you believed needed treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Let me say once again, our influence was non-existent. We could not decide who we would treat, nor how we would treat them. Dr. Relja and I were prisoners like everyone else, the exception being that we were able to go to these buildings sometimes and occasionally to distribute some of the medicines we had to the injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Grubac. Let us go now to a different issue. Were you ever interrogated by military investigators during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion I was called in to the command building and they took a statement from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This happened in the first half of June. I think after my return from the 3rd March school in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said that this happened in the command building. Who called you out of building 22 in order to take you to the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say who were the persons or the person who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man's name was Mladen Zovko and he was nicknamed Kuhar or "the cook".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How were you treated during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: This happened in a room of the command building. During the interrogation were you in a position to see the window of the room -- I mean, do you know where the window of this room was facing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The window of the room was facing building 22 and the yard between the command building and building 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: During the interrogation, were you accused of anything specific?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Mladen Zovko ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me, as far as I can remember -- this was a very brief interview. He may have put three or four questions to me, my name, where I was, what I had been doing in Bradina, and I think that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you sign any piece of paper, a statement after this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that he gave me the statement to sign and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you see where did Mladen Zovko put your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. I think it was in a file of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Going to another issue, Dr. Grubac, were there any women in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were several women in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where were they kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were kept in the building that we called a kind of reception or a guards' room, right next to the entrance to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever visit them in the reception building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I visited them two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any conversation with any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was able to talk to all of them because the guard opened the room and let me in and he did not come in, he waited outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you remember some specific conversation with any of these women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, they told me that I should go there because one of the imprisoned women had some pains because she had a stone in her kidney or something like that, and that is why I had to go there, and indeed on one occasion she did have such pains, so I went back to building 22. We still had some medicines, so I gave her a spasmolytic in the form of a shot, an injection and that is how I spoke to them. I was called in two more times, though I think there was no real reason, because of any disease, but they wanted to get in touch with me to try and learn what would come of them and all of us. On one such occasion, the first time I went, Grozda Cecez told me that all the women were in a very difficult condition and I was able to observe that. They were crying, they were sitting on some kind of shelves. Though I know all those women they did not wish to communicate with them. I had the feeling that they were ashamed, and when I asked Grozda what was wrong with them she told me they were being taken out every night and raped.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, was there ever a period of time when there was no food at all at the camp for the prisoners for some reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the food was very bad, but it was also small in quantity, and it would happen that we would go without food altogether for several days. On one occasion this went on for three or four days. We heard later on in the camp that this was due to something that had happened on the road to Repovci, some policemen had been killed and apparently the people in the camp felt that the Serbs had killed them who were in hiding in the environs of Bradina, but apart from that occasion it would happen several times that we would go without food for two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember any of the women complaining about this lack of food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not remember the women speaking about food in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, did you have any chance to communicate with your wife during your stay in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not communicate with her, but I used some connections I had, if I may call them that, through the guards so I would send her messages, and on one occasion I managed to send her a little letter, a piece of paper telling her not to come to Celebici because something bad could happen to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So you sent a written message. Through whom did you send it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I sent it through a guard whom I had known and who knew her, but I would not like to say his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right, Dr. Grubac. Can you say approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This happened -- the messages, I sent her messages in June and July, but this written note was sent, I think, in the second half of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did your wife ever come to visit you at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she came once.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Only once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the second half of July, prior to my leaving the camp, maybe seven or ten days before I left the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which place inside the camp did you meet your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In one of the premises in the command building.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who called you to go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You got a room in the command building, you told us. Who was in that room when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived there Pavo Mucic was there and my myself, Gordana. I am not sure whether the secretary was there, this woman who was working in the command building. I think she was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic remain there during the conversation between you and your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did the conversation last, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe altogether not more than 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could your wife bring you anything, I mean food or clothes or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She brought some food, maybe a shirt and some underwear, and her sister-in-law came with her. She did not enter the room, but later on she asked Pavo and then he let her come in to visit her husband, that is the brother of my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, in your testimony, you have mentioned today Mr. Hazim Delic. Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew his father Ibro before. I cannot really recall how we met. I think he was treated by my colleague, Ahmed Jusuftbegovic who was a specialist in internal medicine. I may have helped him a little when he was due to retire. His father was a carpenter, so both he and Hazim put some wooden boards in my home, and I also visited them at their home several times because Hazim's mother was ill and I treated her for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Delalic's position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delalic was the deputy commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you mean Delic or Delalic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am talking about Delic. I am sorry. What was Mr. Delic's position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought you were thinking of Delic. He was deputy commander of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards addressed him as such. Nobody told us officially what people's positions were. We learnt this from their behaviour, from the attitudes they had and the way in which the guards addressed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you first came to the camp did you notice anything about his legs? Did he walk normally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A day after my arrival to Celebici I met Hazim Delic in building number 6. Knowing him I thought I could address him and I did, and I told him, "here I am", and whether my colleague Ahmed Jusuftbegovic was aware that I was there and I asked him if he could inform him and help me. At that time he was carrying a crutch under his armpit. He said his leg had been injured; he was limping a little bit and using this crutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You also mentioned Zenga. Did you know him from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never saw him before the war -- rather I did not know him from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you get to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From somebody in the camp. At the time I thought his name was not Esad but Zio, that is why I confuse the two names. That is why I sometimes call him Zio, but we all called him by his nickname Zenga. So I cannot tell you exactly who it was who told me his name was Esad Landzo Zenga. So we knew that. I think there was another guard with the same surname, Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see this other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I really cannot confirm that. I do not even know whether he existed. I seem to recall that he may have existed, but I am not quite sure whether there was another guard by the same surname. But it seems to me that there may have been another one, but I am not sure what is the truth about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever get to know the nickname of this other one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What was the position of Zenga in the camp, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a guard, like all the other guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. You say that building 22 had two windows facing the entrance of tunnel 9. Was the position of these windows such as to allow you to see easily outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually we could not look out easily because the windows were quite high up near the ceiling, so they were not at the normal height as windows in an apartment, they were higher up, nearer the ceiling. But only through the window to the right of the entrance into the hangar could we clearly see the entrance to building number 9, or rather tunnel number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything particular looking out of this window facing tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now that you ask me, I just remembered that this Risto Mrkajic, the young man whose name I could not recall a moment ago, he would often look through the window because his father Nikola Mrkajic was imprisoned in building number 9. He was almost on duty on that window, though other prisoners and patients who were mobile would stand up on their beds and look through the window. We could see sometimes what was happening in front of tunnel number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about you yourself? Did you ever look out of this window and see yourself what happened in front of tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I looked through that window often and I watched what was happening in front of number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what you saw on these occasions when you looked out of the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I saw the guards beating somebody, one of the prisoners from the tunnel, in front of its entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you recognise any of the prisoners being beaten in front of tunnel 9, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not recognise the prisoners that were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you recognise any of the persons beating the prisoners in front of tunnel 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times Hazim Delic was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you see with what did Mr. Delic beat prisoners on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most frequently he beat them with a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say approximately how many times you observed Mr. Delic with that baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him often with a baseball bat. It was like a symbol. He often carried this bat, and I think I saw him twice beating prisoners in front of building number 9 with the baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think that is a convenient place to stop now for the lunch break. We will come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. You may proceed, Mr. Turone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Dr. Grubac, during the whole of your stay at Celebici, what did you observe being actually Mr. Mucic's role in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Objection, your Honours. The witness has already answered this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My idea is that we have been asking about the very first day in which capacity he did something, but if this is enough, I will go to another question. I want now to have him explain what else he might have observed during the whole of his stay at Celebici about the role of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you disagree that he has answered the question before?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: No, I agree that he has answered the question before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any other subsequent questions? It is not necessary to ask the same question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I will pass to another question, your Honour. How frequently did you see Mr. Mucic in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him very frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What could you observe him doing at the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the position where I was I could not see what he was doing unless I saw him in front of the command building, or if he was entering our building number 22. He had, and I will explain this, a bit -- he was wont to come to building 22, the guards would then open the metal door. He would say "keep the door open that way" and we also liked it, because in that way the space could be ventilated at least a little and we could see what was happening in front of the building. Sometimes he would come inside to building 22. He would greet me and Dr. Relja and sometimes some of the injured people and often he would shoot at a paper target in front of the building from a pistol. Sometimes vehicles with foreign licences -- he would come to the camp in a vehicle with foreign licence plates, sometimes on a motorbike, and he also had his driver driving a van which he used, and it also served for other transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was he usually in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not usually, he was always in camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have occasions to talk to him often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would often say hello, he would ask a question or two when he came into building number 22. Twice he asked me to come to the building where the camp command was. Both times inter alia he asked me if I knew, if I had known from before Jasmin Guska, the head of the MUP, and whether he had been my patient and whether he was a sane person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How often did Mr. Mucic come to building 22 approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came often, I could not say the exact number of times, but he would drop in quite frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just to say hello to you or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember him coming for any other reason except to say hello. I do not know what other intentions he might have had, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When Mr. Mucic came to building 22, did he ask any questions concerning how persons received their injuries, either to you or to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He never asked that, such questions. I personally gained the impression that he was not interested at all in that. I even gained the impression that he was not at all interested generally in what was happening in that building. He never asked any question from which I could conclude that he was interested in anything regarding the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he ever bring any medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember whether he ever brought any medicines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you ever ask him to bring medicines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we were in no position to ask for anything from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. You indicated previously that on 22nd July, you were permitted to leave the camp. Can you describe in detail what happened that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day some time after noon, in the afternoon in fact, Zejnil Delalic came to the camp. Some of the guards came to building 22 and asked me to come to the command building. I went there in one of the official rooms. I found Zejnil Delalic and Hazim Delic. We greeted each other and Delalic asked Hazim to leave the room because he had to talk to me about something. Hazim left the room and I myself and Zejnil Delalic remained in the room. He asked me how I was, what I was doing, and he said that my wife had called and she had asked him to come and talk to me and to see whether he could release me from the camp. He said that she could not come immediately -- that he could not come immediately, that he would come in a few days, and he also added that she had called some seven or six days before that. But he also added that he was not able to come before he came, and he said "I have now taken this opportunity to come and talk to you to see what is in your file and to see whether I can have you released". He then told me that he had inspected my file, he had a folder in front of him and he said to me, "in this file, there is nothing special, so I will release you from the camp". He also told me, "tonight they will come to take you and take you out of the camp", so I said goodbye to him and I returned to building number 22. He also told me that he would also release Dr. Relja Mrkajic. I returned to building number 22. There I talked to the injured people a bit. I told them that Zejnil Delalic had come and he had said he would release me and Relja and as of that night, they would probably remain alone. In the evening on that same day, I cannot exactly say at what time precisely, perhaps at 9.00 or 10.00 pm, a Jeep came, Zejnil Delalic's Jeep. They opened the door to the building and some of the guards filled into these charge documents which he gave us and said to us, "you as doctors have every reason to buy drinks for everyone. You are leaving the camp". He gave two slips of paper to me and Dr. Mrkajic. He told us, "get ready, get your things if you have any, collect your things and now you will be taken home".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Before going on in this account, Dr. Grubac, how long did the conversation with Mr. Delalic last in the command building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately at what time did the guard come to you then later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around 9.00 or 10.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said he had two documents concerning you and Dr. Relja Mrkajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which documents were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were our discharge papers, and I sent a photostated copy of my discharge document to this Tribunal when they asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: By whom was this release document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The discharge documents were signed by Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Now may I ask this document to be marked for identification with number, I believe, 169. The document was already provided to the Defence lawyers, with copies for your Honours. (Handed). Please put the document on the ELMO and show it to the witness. Dr. Grubac, would you please look at this document and tell the court whether you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the certificate that I was released from the Celebici prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Is this the paper you received from the guard the evening of July 22nd?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is a copy of the paper which I received in the evening of July 22nd in building 22 in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I tender Exhibit 169 for admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: On this document, Dr. Grubac, what does the handwriting "Konjic Celebici" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That means that my movement was limited only to the area of Konjic, Celebici, and that I was not to leave Konjic or move along any other route.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do the two handwritten lines mean, I mean the ones at the bottom of the paper, near the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They mean that -- Zejnil explained it to us that we would rest at our homes for 10 or 15 days or so and that afterwards they would come for us and drive us to the Celebici camp to care about the health of the prisoners and inmates in that compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. What happened to you after you had received the release documents from the guard. You were talking about a Jeep. Please go ahead with your account, very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We gathered the few things that we had in plastic bags. We said goodbye to the injured patients, and we sat in this Jeep which used to drive Zejnil Delalic earlier and which he had sent for us and the driver took us to Zejnil Delalic's house in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean both you and Dr. Relja Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you describe the house of Mr. Delalic and where it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The house of Zejnil Delalic is in the town of Konjic, at the exit towards the south, under the city motel on the down side of the petrol station, at the exit of the city of Konjic towards the city of Mostar, and the river Nerveta flows across the house on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What happened when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We entered through a metal gate into the yard of the house and the driver and the guard took us up these stairs and inside the house of Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you meet Mr. Delalic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Zejnil Delalic waited for us in the house, received us in his house and his brother Dzemal was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Zejnil Delalic exactly tell you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He greeted us, he told us to take a seat and we sat in the sitting room of his house. He offered us drinks, we had some drinks. He told us that now we were out of the camp that we needed to rest for a while and that they would start coming for us again to take us to Celebici to see to the health of the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was it on this occasion that he explained to you the meaning of the two handwritten lines at the bottom of the release document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember the details exactly. I think he told us that we would be at our homes, that we needed to look after ourselves, then take care we could not leave Konjic. We could only be in Konjic and Celebici and he also asked Dr. Relja Mrkajic, and Dr. Relja Mrkajic asked Delalic to change the setup because he did not have a place to stay in Konjic, and he would stay with his relatives in Ostrozac, so that he could move from Ostrozac to Celebici. I believe Zejnil corrected this on the certificate or agreed that that would be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How long did this conversation last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did not last long, we had a drink, whiskey or coffee, some other drink perhaps. We talked a bit, then the driver took me to the flat of the parents of my wife and Relja to the flat of some friends of his. I think it did not last more than half a hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, did you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic from before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, I knew him much earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you explain how you knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a number of joint friends, we met occasionally, and these shared friends of ours came with me to his house -- I came with them to his house several times and I knew some members of his family. I knew a brother of his who I had treated. Once or twice I had been to the house of his parents and perhaps also the house of his sister, and we perhaps also met in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, was there a time when you were interviewed by the Bosnian television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot locate it exactly in terms of time. The arrival of Bosnian television to the camp in Celebici; I cannot say whether this was in July or possibly in August after I had been released from the camp and when I came to the camp to treat the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where inside the camp did this TV interview take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether the TV crew with a camera entered the building, I think they did. They filmed the interior of the building and in front of building 22 they talked to me and Relja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the journalists or journalist who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember the name of the journalist. I do not remember the name of the cameraman and the other technical crew members. This was a crew of Jadranka Milosevic and Zvonko Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were they two men or a man and a woman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jadranka Milosevic is a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did anybody ask you to give this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand you well. You mean before they came or when they were there, whether I would grant them an interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Either before or at the moment they were there; did anybody come and tell you you should give an interview to Bosnian television, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How come, how did that happen that this TV crew arrived and interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really do not know how to explain this, how they came, who called them, who invited them, how they came to the camp. I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did the journalist directly come to you and ask you to give the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With them were Zejnil Delalic and Pavo Mucic. I do not know for sure which one of them said, I believe it was Zejnil or Pavo, he said, "this is a TV crew. You will be interviewed and they will film the building", and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic do during the interview? Were they present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Zejnil was present for a time, I cannot recall for sure. Then he left, I believe, the command building, but Pavo was present all the time and he was also filming something during this interview with his own camera, while they were filming, the crew, I mean. He had a camera of his own and he was filming us and them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did any of them, either Mr. Mucic and Mr. Delalic, also give an interview to this TV crew, as far as you could personally observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were giving this interview they were not interviewed. Maybe before or after they had finished with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What questions did the journalist ask you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The questions were something like this, how many injured there were, how they had been injured, how long they have been treated, what their present condition was, do we have medicines, what is the situation in the building. Those were the questions, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you answer to those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We answered as they expected us to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you always answer the truth to her questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, partly what we said was true, such as the things -- where the injured had come from, how badly injured they were and that sort of thing, but the rest, we answered according to their expectations, because we feared the consequences, which means our other replies were not truthful or correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you specifically remember some specific question to which you answered the truth and some specific question to which you gave an untruthful answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered truthfully when I said that the injured were there, who had been injured when being brought to the Celebici, who had been injured and beaten in the camp and in the sports hall in Konjic. As for the other questions, whether we had the medicines we needed, how they felt, what the situation was like, that I did not answer correctly. I said that we had medicines, that the situation was good, that their condition was good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Why did you answer that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had some experience from the camp from before that if anyone were to say something that was true or tried to tell the truth, he was punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately how long did the interview last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They filmed the building itself inside, then they spoke to us and after that we all sat in one of the rooms in the command building. This whole thing may have lasted up to one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What about sitting in the command building? Who was present there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reporters were there, Ms. Milosevic and Mr. Maric, then there was Zejnil Delalic, Pavo Mucic. I do not remember exactly whether Delic was there or anyone else. There were some other people, some other assistants there, the cameraman and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You said Mr. Mucic was filming the interview with his own camera. Was this the only time you saw Mr. Mucic filming with his own camera inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion he was filming, but I also saw him carrying the camera, so that I think in addition to that time, I did see him carrying the camera or putting it into his car or taking it out of his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Did you observe Mr. Zejnil Delalic being present at the camp in other occasions besides the ones you have already described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zejnil would come to the camp occasionally because, as I have just described, we could peep under the door and see a part of the plateau between the command building and our own building, and occasionally the door was open so that we could see who was coming in or going out of those buildings. On several occasions, I might say, several times we saw his car. It was a white Jeep, and also I saw him accompanied by some other uniformed men entering the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how many times you might have seen Mr. Delalic in the camp in this way on these occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you the exact number. I would say several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any other conversation with him inside the camp besides what you said already?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, later on I and my wife went to his house and spoke to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I am saying inside Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have any personal contact with Zejnil Delalic in the camp except for the one I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You have indicated that you continued to treat prisoners in Celebici after your release. How did you get to the camp on those occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most often Pavo Mucic's driver Buric would come with a van to pick me up and drive me to Celebici, and once or twice Hazim Delic came to pick me up, and Pavo came twice also, as he was going to the camp, he took me with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you going daily to the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This lasted -- this did not last very long, maybe ten days, maybe every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So it was not on a daily basis during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps during that period of ten days I skipped one day, but otherwise it was daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In this period of time, were you transported together with Dr. Relja Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you explain how come this lasted only ten days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that I was told that there was no need for me to go to the Celebici camp, but it would be easier for them to pick up Dr. Relja Mrkajic in Ostrozac because it was closer and take him to Celebici and that I should go to the camp in the sports hall in Konjic and treat the prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You say that a couple of times you were transported to Celebici by Mr. Mucic. Did he used to drive you directly to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, both times he stopped in front of Zejnil Delalic's house, went inside to Zejnil Delalic's house, stayed there for about 10 or 15 minutes, then came back and we would continue the ride to Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic ever say anything to you during these drives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would talk informally. He would joke sometimes and on one occasion he said that he had certain obligations with respect to Zejnil, that Zejnil had helped him when he needed it, when he went to work to Germany and Austria and that he felt to a certain extent indebted to Zejnil Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Dr. Grubac, did you have any further occasion to see Mr. Zejnil Delalic after all this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We were saying something about your wife and you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I thought you meant in the camp itself. No, after that I saw Zejnil Delalic once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was somewhere around September 1992, perhaps the second half of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was staying at my in-laws, their apartment in Konjic and because of the situation we were in we were trying to find a way of getting out of Konjic. We knew that we could not leave without somebody's assistance, so my wife and I agreed, and on the basis of our contact with some people, we came to the conclusion that Zejnil could help us to leave Konjic. So we called up on the phone several times and my wife managed, through his secretary, to schedule an appointment; actually he said he would receive us one evening in September, I think it was in the second half of September, that we should come to his home at a fixed time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you go to his home for this appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my wife and I went there on that day in the evening to Zejnil Delalic's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did you want to tell him exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We simply wanted to ask him to help us so that my wife, my children and I could leave Konjic and cross over into liberated territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Why did you choose exactly Mr. Delalic to ask that and not another person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we believed that Delalic was a person who had it in his power to do it, and on the other hand, we believed that he would want to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Delalic answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We came to his home, we sat there for a while. We talked to him. We joked a little perhaps, and we told him what the purpose of our visit was. We told him quite frankly that we would like to leave Konjic. He said that perhaps I might be able to leave, that he could fix that since I had been in the camp, but that it would be more difficult to arrange for my wife and children to leave. I joked then and said, "well that is no problem, put my wife and children in the camp then they will be detainees as well and you will have no problems with them". Then he told us to wait a little to see whether it could be done, and then he asked me, "why do you want to leave Konjic? Let me fix it so that you can work in our military hospital in Igman or Tarcin". I said that I would not like to work in those hospitals, but that all that I was asking was for him to help us leave Konjic. He did not promise to do that and that is how we left. What he said was "well, we will see what can be done".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you get to know what was Mr. Delalic's official position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, talking to Delalic he joked a little and he showed us some papers, a fax message, I think it was, sent to him by people from Borci, from the Serbian held territory. He said, "look how many commanders have signed" as if there were several thousand of them over there, whereas I know in fact there are much less. Then he showed us some extracts from the newspapers where the Croats had criticised him, and I cannot remember whether at the top of the fax it said "to the commander of the first tactical group: Zejnil Delalic", or was this written on one of the answers he was sending to them as the signature, "commander of the first tactical group". I think that also the articles he showed us from the newspapers referred to him as the commander of the First Tactical Group. In any event, that was the first time that I saw this post being described as commander of the First Tactical Group of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Early on when we went to see him, we did not go there because we knew that that was his position, but simply because we had learnt from our communication with others that he had the power to help us, but it was then that I learnt that he was commander of the First Tactical Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Why did Mr. Delalic show these papers to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was showing us these excerpts to complain why the Croats were criticising him and these others also to joke that the Serbian Army from Borci had signed a paper with so many signatures, as if to show that they were so strong, whereas in fact he knew they were much less powerful.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Grubac. I have no other questions in examination-in-chief, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How are you arranging your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We will proceed in this way, your Honours: first counsel for Mr. Delalic, second counsel for Mr. Mucic, third counsel for Mr. Delic and fourth counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Dr. Grubac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you probably know my name is Edina Residovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Mr. Grubac, before I start with my questions I usually warn the witness of a fact which is very important to be able to follow these proceedings and for a better understanding of my questions and your answers; namely the two of us speak the same language that we understand, and it would be very easy for us to communicate quickly with my questions and your answers. However, the court, for whose benefit you are here, has to know what we are talking about, and it is therefore necessary for every question and every answer to be translated, so I would like to ask you, when I finish my question, for you to wait until you hear in the earphones the English translation of my question, after which, will you please answer that question and I too will behave accordingly. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, in the course of the direct examination you said that you originally came from Montenegro but that you spent a long time living in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am originally from Montenegro, but I lived in Konjic from 1965 until 1992. That is where I formed my family as well, and probably I would still be there if what happened had not happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Most of that time you spent in Konjic as a doctor, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout your time in Konjic, you were working as a doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For a time you were also the general manager of the health centre in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time the health centre had about 50 doctors and dentists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you mean when you say "then" "?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were the manager.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the more remote areas of the municipality you had local outpatients wards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a doctor and the manager of the health centre you virtually visited every nook and corner of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were familiar with many people in Konjic and also a large number of citizens of Konjic knew you well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were personally acquainted with many, if one might call them so, important people in Konjic who performed important political public offices in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You yourself were a prominent figure in your town, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure I would describe myself as being very committed, but I was committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were so involved that you were familiar with the structure of the main bodies in the municipalities and the main holders of offices in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, you too, as a prestigious doctor and the manager of the health centre, you were one of the more prominent figures in the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One might put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the outbreak of the war you were replaced or you abandoned your position as doctor and it was then that Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic was appointed manager, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic was your friend and the witness at your wedding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He is one of your friends who, like you, was a friend of Mr. Delalic's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Delalic was acquainted with and was friendly with some other doctors from your health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that as early as April 1992 it became clear to many people, including yourself, that this area of Konjic would also be swept by some unwelcome and perhaps war operations, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you belong to those citizens of Konjic who tried, nevertheless, despite the circumstances, to restore balance to interethnic relationships and to prevent a conflict breaking out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some people formally organised themselves to do something in that direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was along those lines that the forum of citizens was formed, which included a number of prominent figures, journalists, doctors, public figures and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you, too, were a member of that forum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Grubac, you must certainly know that already in the first half of April a large number of inhabitants, Serbs from Konjic, started to leave and to group together in certain areas of the municipality such as Donje Selo, Bradina, Borci and other local communities or villages in which the Serbs had a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but I would add that this was not being done only by Serbs but that this was also being done by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know that that was the time when some adverse events were taking place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, due to which a state of imminent danger of war is proclaimed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of those conditions, the state and the authorities probably seek to make sure that able bodied men do not depart from their places of residence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not put it in the way that you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the local authorities in Konjic started to prevent this movement of the population and that a decision to that effect was passed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware that this was done at the level of the authorities, but that they did restrict movement, that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as a person who was active you must have known that in mid April a general mobilisation was proclaimed in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was exactly the date you have given, but I know that there was some kind of a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, you have stated to the court in the way you have described it that you were living and working in Konjic up until 6th or 7th May when, with your wife, you went to Bradina where your children were already, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps one might explain this a little. On 6th or 7th May I did not go to Bradina, I went to Bradina for the holidays, for the May day holidays to visit my children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But that is when you stopped going to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the 6th or 7th, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view that after May 1st until the 6th or 7th you went to Konjic, you certainly witnessed the daily shelling of the town which began on May 4th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think this is too general when you say "daily shelling", but on one of those days before 6th or 7th May, I was told that two shells had fallen on Konjic, one down town and one near the railway station. During my sojourn in the town, and I stayed there for several hours, there was no shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where those shells came from that hit the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From which positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware of any positions around Konjic, nor did I know where the shells were coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that there were positions in the direction of the lake of Borci, what would be your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, as you have testified in court, you were also in Konjic, and you must have witnessed the shelling of the town throughout 1992, and that it suffered terribly from the consequences of that shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, May 6th to 7th, you probably were aware of a heavy artillery and air and missile attack on the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. On 6th or 7th May I returned to Bradina by bus. This must have been around noon, and on that day there was no attack, up to the time I left. What happened later I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told the court that you knew that the inhabitants of Bradina, the Serbs, had organised themselves, and they had some kind of guard duty and some checkpoints. Since you were up there in Bradina, can you tell us whether such checkpoints existed along the highway which you know is the only asphalt road between Konjic and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was one checkpoint held by the Muslims and the Croats south of the tunnel at the entrance to Bradina, and the other one was on the north side of the tunnel in the direction of Bradina which was held by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you told me a moment ago that you were familiar with the setup of the authorities in the municipality, you must have known that in the military structure in the former SFRY, there was the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I know Territorial Defence is one of the elements not of national Defence but in addition to the JNA, it was part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. There was the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence as a second element.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably know, Mr. Grubac, that earlier the SUP, the Secretariat of the Interior, which would mean the police forces in the broadest sense, later changed its name to MUP, which is to say the Ministry of the Interior, which as an institution performed the duties of police and internal security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you probably are acquainted, Mr. Grubac, with the fact that after Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaimed an independent state, the Territorial Defence was proclaimed a legitimate defensive force of that state, and that the Ministry of Internal Affairs continued to discharge its statutorily described functions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not so. This is oversimplified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, then we will ask someone who is more versed in those things than you or myself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You ask me whether I know that that was so and I am just replying, no, I am not aware of the fact that it was so, which does not mean that I am an expert on the subject, but I believed that it is different and that Territorial Defence could not be proclaimed an armed force of a state because it is already part of the composition of the armed forces of the state in that particular state of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us skip over these political subjects which are of less interest to us. I should like to ask you to confirm some facts for me, and you have stated your opinion vis-a-vis this particular question, thank you. I should only like to ask you if it is true that in the city of Konjic, there remained certain structures or certain bodies of authority which had existed also before, and continued to discharge their functions also at that time; which is to say the MUP, the assembly, the war presidency, so these structures existed at the time you left Konjic, did they not, when you left for Bradina; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically, they existed, but probably without there being members of all the nations in them. I believe at that time already representatives of the Serb nation had already left these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These authorities in Konjic as -- as regards these authorities in Konjic, do you know of their having issued an order to Serbian guards to dismantle the checkpoints which they had erected in the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Will you please be so kind as to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the authorities in Konjic asked the Serbs in Bradina to dismantle the checkpoints and free the road and asked the men to surrender the weapons which they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer in the affirmative that particular question. I can say however that a group of people from Bradina did go to have some negotiations with the Muslims and the Croats in Podorasac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Grubac, you know Rajko Djordjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He worked in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence of Konjic, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was not expelled from the headquarters, he left it of his own volition and came to the city, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. He was in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was in charge of organising a defence and assisting the people in procuring arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for the second part, I do not know about the procuring of arms, I really do not know how one could go about providing arms in Bradina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that he was in charge of organising the Defence of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you have already replied to the Prosecutor's question, you did not want to get involved in such activities yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just supplement this. Defence is a broad term. I believe there were some village guard duties which were there to protect my people, the elderly, the women, the children from some attackers. That was not Defence in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment. I am not sure, your Honour, the witness understood that he should listen for the English translation coming out of the other set of earphones to end before he answers his question. I am not even sure the other set of earphones is set on the English. We are getting into that problem of everything running together again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There is perhaps an inconsistency between the question and answer. Perhaps that might help us to correct it. But I see some correlation between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, we have been warned. Our colleagues would like us to slow down a bit. You were not entrusted with -- you were not given any sort of weapon, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you knew that the majority of the population of Bradina did have weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That the majority of the population had weapons? No, that is not true. Only some of the people in Bradina had some armaments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, can you confirm that by May 25th, the day you say that Bradina came under an attack, the checkpoints held by those guards in Bradina had not been dismantled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether they were or not. These checkpoints are quite a distance from the centre of the town and I did not go there so I cannot confirm what you have just stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you probably know since you did go down town to work at the infirmary, to the centre of Bradina, that the road was not -- the blockade of the road had not been lifted by that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it had been deblocked because before that somebody had blocked the tunnel on the side towards Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some people in Konjic associated you and your activities in Bradina with the family of your wife and some persons who also bore your surname, although they were no relatives of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is Rajko Djordjic related to your wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Rajko Djordjic is a relative of my wife's.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the Republika Serbska in the Hercegovina there is a general Grubac who is no relative of yours. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of these two facts, do you think or have you been told that some people associated your position in Bradina with the fact that your wife is related to Rajko Djordjic who organised the Defence of Bradina and also with the fact that in positions held by the JNA army or the Republika Serbska army at that time is General Grubac. Did anyone inform you of this fact or do you believe your position had been associated with these facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is possible, but I was not told that by anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have told me, as a physician and the manager of the health centre, you knew the community, the commune of Konjic and Bradina is certainly part of the municipality of Konjic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell us why the authorities of Konjic should occupy by armed force the territory of its own municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see how I could explain that to you. I believe that that is exactly where the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did there exist a normal passage through Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The tunnel on one side of Bradina had been blown up, mined, so one could not pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Except by a detour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by a detour, but I am not sure of it, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Dr. Grubac, you can confirm the fact that there was a mixed ethnic composition in Konjic with the majority being Muslims, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of the 45,000 inhabitants of the municipality of Konjic, Muslims accounted for 52 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But the regions, the areas and the villages surrounding Konjic had a majority Serbian population for the most part, Donje Selo, Bjelovcina, Brdjani, Bradina, Bjelasnica, Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Celebici too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Celebici too. If these areas I have just enumerated were to be separated from the commune of Konjic, then the centre of the city of Konjic will be completely cut off from the other parts of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina: Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know to whom it would occur to separate these Serbian villages from the municipality of Konjic because as you are yourself perfectly aware, these are villages which are part of the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But I am asking you if it did occur to you, probably not to you or to me, or if it did occur to someone, if someone had that wish or intention to separate this territory of the villages surrounding Konjic from the municipality of Konjic, would it not be true in that true that the centre of the city of Konjic would be completely cut off from the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically that is true, but these villages cannot be separated from Konjic because around them we have another ring of Muslim and Croat villages surrounding these villages, but theoretically that is correct. Possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Theoretically, if that theory were translated into practice and someone were to take such a decision, from the stand point of the legal authorities, such an act on the part of the population would be a rebellion and an anticonstitutional act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on 22nd March the SDS adopted a decision to establish the Serbian commune of Konjic which reflected precisely what we have just now agreed from the standpoint of legitimate authorities as being impossible, which commune incorporated all these regions that we have enumerated. The decision was made on 22nd March 1992 and later endorsed by a decision of the SDS in the commune of Konjic about their non-participation in the Defence of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see through what means or media I could have found out that anyone had adopted such a decision, and I do not know of such a decision. I have not heard of one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the political leadership in Bradina was fully under the influence of the SDS party to which you did not belong yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not confirm that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some 600 to 700 inhabitants lived in Bradina before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time when you came to Bradina, there were over 1,500 inhabitants there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that there were 1,500 of them, but there were many more than the usual number of inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me the number of militarily able-bodied men? What was their number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not engage in any such statistics. I really could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you certainly do not know what the number of children or women was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I do not know the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many armed persons there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know. I was in no structure that dealt with these things, no body which dealt with these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many men from Bradina had been arrested and taken to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what time you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During those battles, attacks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that all the male population, irrespective of age, was apprehended and taken to either Celebici or the sports hall in Musala or the 3rd March primary school or perhaps some other facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You cannot say what the number was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Okay, let us return to your personal position. After your arrival in Bradina, in consultation with Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic you continued to work in the health centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no agreement with Dr. Ahmed Jusufbegovic for me to continue to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Relja have such approval?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was of your own initiative that together with Dr. Relja and Dr. Zuza that you continued working in the infirmary in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 6th or 7th May I could no longer return because the Muslim held checkpoint under Bradina, southwards towards Konjic. They would not let the buses pass so I could not go any further. They had also abolished the bus line on which I used to go from Bradina to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubac, that is an answer to the question why you did not return to Konjic. I am asking you something else; did you, together with Dr. Relja Mrkajic and Dr. Zuza, continue to work in the infirmary in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not continue. I started to work in that facility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your precision. Let me just ask you a few questions regarding this infirmary which I do know in a way, but it is better for you to tell the court. This is a small branch infirmary which has two separated but linked rooms. You and Dr. Relja worked in one of those and Dr. Zuza in the other room; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your room was the general practice infirmary and Dr. Zuza's was the dentist's surgery; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the day of the attack on Bradina in this infirmary, were you yourself and Dr. Relja and Dr. Zuza, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And some of the medical staff, the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. During the day already an injured villager, a local, came to the infirmary and you extended aid to him; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were informed after that there were people injured on both sides so you went there and together you also treated the other patients, extended aid to the other patients, Suljina Strana?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You and Dr. Relja, although it was offered to you, never wanted to accept weapons, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not so. No one ever offered me any weapons. As a matter of fact, I do not know how to use any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that Dr. Relja had no weapons, you know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dr. Relja had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that Dr. Zuza had a semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know that Dr. Zuza had a semi-automatic rifle. How should I know that?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that that semi-automatic rifle was kept in the dentistry, in the dentist's surgery in the infirmary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as far as I know in the dentist's surgery there were no weapons or any rifles, unless it was concealed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have probably heard that Dr. Zuza after he had been arrested, surrendered his semi-automatic rifle from the dental surgery?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of you, from you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If Dr. Relja Mrkajic were to testify before this court to these facts about which I have just asked you, would you consider them not to be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not say that at all, I was not there when they were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but if the doctor confirms that he had that rifle in the dental surgery, you say that is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, what I am saying is that when I came into the dental surgery, which was not all that often, there was no rifle in sight. There might have been one hidden.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During that day, the first day of the attack on Bradina, as well as later, you did not see anyone that you could recognise among those who were attacking Bradina; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
